Contributing to the accident were ambiguous air traffic control practices, unclear and inconsistently understood definitions surrounding approach clearances and radar arrivals, and the absence of standardized phrasiology that clearly assigned responsibility for terrain clearance. The design of the approach charts and the common dive and drive techniques of the era further encouraged early descent once a clearance had been received. And with no ground proximity warning systems on board, there was nothing to warn the pilots when a mistake ultimately had been made. And this was where the first major changes came in. The investigators concluded that the fraiology that the pilots and the controllers used to communicate was not precise enough for the environment they were operating in and that this ambiguity had now become a hazard. In response, the FAA moved to standardize aviation phrasiology so that critical instructions would carry the same meaning to every pilot and controller every time. By the end of 1975, the FAA had developed and issued a common pilot air traffic control lexicon, formally defining the meaning of approach clearances, altitude assignments, radar services, and the responsibilities attached to each. The investigators also concluded that the accident exposed multiple gaps where the system had relied on assumptions instead of safeguards and those gaps were now slowly closed one by one. The FAA, for example, issued new guidance assigning controllers with the responsibility to warn flight crews if the radar indicated that they were at an unsafe altitude, even if the aircraft was technically navigating on its own. And at the same time, new regulations clarified exactly what altitude of flight was required to maintain after receiving an approach clearance, removing the ambiguity that allowed cleared for approach to be interpreted as permission to descent early. But just as importantly, this accident also highlighted how often crews and controllers recognized dangerous patterns but had no safe way to report them. So in response, the industry helped establish an anonymous aviation safety reporting system administered by NASA that allows pilots, controllers, and engineers to submit safety reports without fear of discipline or retaliation. Now, that system is still used today and has fundamentally changed how hazards are identified, allowing patterns to be addressed before they turn into accidents. Now, I have spoken before about how important these kinds of systems are and how giving crews a venue to speak up without fear of reprisal is really the bedrock of aviation safety. But another change that came from this accident possibly had an even more dramatic impact on the aviation world. You see, as a direct result of this accident, the FAA in 1975 made GPWS mandatory for any airliner with more than nine seats. So with that, the combination of standardized communication and an onboard system that could shout out over a quiet cockpit >> changed the entire shape of aviation safety. In the long arc of commercial aviation, GPWS and its newer variant, the EGPWS, are widely seen as the single most important safety features ever adopted. And this means that even though you might not have heard about this accident before because of the improvements it led to, it might well be the single most significant accident that I have ever covered. Namely, that if the engine core was allowed to wind down to zero, it could face something called a core lock. And what a core lock basically is is that it has to do with an air seal inside of the high pressure turbine. Now this air seal it um directs air flow and cooling inside of the engine. And because it does that it has to be really really tight. And the way it's constructed is it has a rotating part and a static part. Now the rotating part has some teeth in it that grinds little grooves in the softer static part around it and generally during normal engine operation the uh the margins are really really tight. Now what can happen if the engine is running at a really high temperature and then suddenly gets cooled down is that the softer surrounding static material will cool down quicker than the rotating part of the air seal. And when that happens, the rotating part can move outside of those grooves that it has been grinding and into new material in the soft material. And at the same time, the softer material since it's cooling down quicker is contracting around the rotating part, greatly increasing the um friction inside of the engine. If the N2 rotation, so the high pressure part inside of the engine is allowed to come to a complete stop, this can actually lock the engine up until the internal components have cooled enough for them to release from each other. And this is why, remember how I said earlier in the video that it was so important that the air speed was kept at a minimum of 240 knots? Well, that's because at 240 knots, there's enough air running through the core of the engine to keep this air seal rotating while it's being cooled down. Then, as it has cooled down properly and you start restart the engine, you will not have a problem. But as you know on this particular occasion since the pilots had forced the aircraft up to 41,000 ft and allowed the air speed to come down that slow it meant that the engines were operating at almost full power heating them up greatly without getting much cooling air running through the core.
